segments.text: Welcome! I'm {{presenter}}, and together we'll make Scrum genuinely click. Scrum is a lightweight framework for building complex products when you can't predict everything up front. It's a framework, not a fixed method: it gives you only the essentials, and your team fills in the rest. It works because of one idea — empiricism: we learn from what actually happens and adjust, instead of following a fixed plan off a cliff. Empiricism stands on three pillars: transparency, we make the work visible; inspection, we check it often; and adaptation, we change course when we learn something.

Now, who does the work? In Scrum there's one Scrum Team — usually ten people or fewer, no sub-teams, no bosses inside it. It's cross-functional, so together they have every skill needed, and self-managing, so they decide how to do the work. There are three accountabilities. First, the Product Owner — accountable for the value of the product, the What and the Why; they own the Product Backlog, and it's one person, not a committee. Second, the Scrum Master, who owns how we work — a coach who serves the team and clears impediments, not a project manager or a boss. Third, the Developers, who own how to build it — the cross-functional group who turn ideas into a usable Increment every Sprint. The three sit as equals; no one commands the others.

One more thing: the five Scrum Values — Commitment, Focus, Openness, Respect, and Courage. They sound soft, but they're the glue. Without openness there's no transparency; without courage nobody raises the hard truth in a retrospective. Live the values, and everything else in Scrum starts to work. Quick check: who decides what the team builds next? The Product Owner. And who removes a blocker slowing the team down? The Scrum Master helps with that.

draw.text: The values build the trust that makes empiricism work.

items.prompt: Match each responsibility to the accountability that owns it.
